entries.8c9e33f337387c6d2e39dd4e8e617551d56d6831: <div sID="gen11501" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="61" osisID="Ps.61" sID="Ps.61"/> <div eID="gen11501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11502" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11503" type="x-p"/> David, in this psalm, as in many others, begins with a sad heart, but concludes with an air of pleasantness—begins with prayers and tears, but ends with songs of praise. Thus the soul, by being lifted up to God, returns to the enjoyment of itself. It should seem David was driven out and banished when he penned this psalm, whether by Saul or Absalom is uncertain: some think by Absalom, because he calls himself "the king" (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.6">ver. 6</reference>), but that refers to the King Messiah. David, in this psalm, resolves to persevere in his duty, encouraged thereto both by his experience an by his expectations. I. He will call upon God because God had protected him, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1-Ps.61.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He will call upon God because God had provided well for him, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.4-Ps.61.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. He will praise God because he had an assurance of the continuance of God's favour to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.6-Ps.61.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. So that, in singing this psalm, we may find that which is very expressive both of our faith and of our hope, of our prayers and of our praises; and some passages in this psalm are very peculiar.
entries.2ade8795033679bdf1f2b813ba72f2b642a038e3: <div eID="gen11503" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11502" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Crying to God in Distress.</title> <div sID="gen11504" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear my cry, O God; attend unto my prayer. 2 From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock <hi type="italic">that</hi> is higher than I. <hi type="super">3</hi> For thou hast been a shelter for me, <hi type="italic">and</hi> a strong tower from the enemy. <hi type="super">4</hi> I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings. Selah. <div eID="gen11504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11505" type="x-p"/> In these verses we may observe, <div eID="gen11505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11506" type="x-p"/> I. David's close adherence and application to God by prayer in the day of his distress and trouble: "Whatever comes, <hi type="italic">I will cry unto thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.2">v. 2</reference>),—not cry unto other gods, but to thee only,—not fall out with thee because thou afflictest me, but still look unto thee, and wait upon thee,—not speak to thee in a cold and careless manner, but cry to thee with the greatest importunity and fervency of spirit, as one that will not let thee go except thou bless me." This he will do, 1. Notwithstanding his distance from the sanctuary, the house of prayer, where he used to attend as in the court of requests: "<hi type="italic">From the end of the earth,</hi> or of <hi type="italic">the land,</hi> from the most remote and obscure corner of the country, <hi type="italic">will I cry unto thee.</hi>" Note, Wherever we are we may have liberty of access to God, and may find a way open to the throne of grace. <hi type="italic">Undique ad c&#339;los tantundem est viæ—Heaven is equally accessible from all places.</hi> "Nay, because I am here in the end of the earth, in sorrow and solitude, therefore <hi type="italic">I will cry unto thee.</hi>" Note, That which separates us from our other comforts should drive us so much the nearer to God, the fountain of all comfort. 2. Notwithstanding the dejection and despondency of his spirit: "Though <hi type="italic">my heart is overwhelmed,</hi> it is not so sunk, so burdened, but that it may be lifted up to God in prayer; if it is not capable of being thus raised, it is certainly too much cast down. Nay, because my heart is ready to be overwhelmed, therefore <hi type="italic">I will cry unto thee,</hi> for by that means it will be supported and relived." Note, Weeping must quicken praying, and not deaden it. <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted? Let him pray,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jam. v. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Ps. cii., title</reference>. <div eID="gen11506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11507" type="x-p"/> II. The particular petition he put up to God when his heart was overwhelmed and he was ready to sink: <hi type="italic">Lead me to the rock that is higher than I;</hi> that is, 1. "To the rock which is too high for me to get up to unless thou help me to it. Lord, give me such an assurance and satisfaction of my own safety as I can never attain to but by thy special grace working such a faith in me." 2. "To the rock on the top of which I shall be set further out of the reach of my troubles, and nearer the serene and quiet region, than I can be by any power or wisdom of my own." God's power and promise are a rock that is higher than we. This rock is Christ; those are safe that are in him. We cannot get upon this rock unless God by his power lead us. <hi type="italic">I will put thee in the cleft of the rock,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.33.22">Exod. xxxiii. 22</reference>. We should therefore by faith and prayer put ourselves under the divine management, that we may be taken under the divine protection. <div eID="gen11507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11508" type="x-p"/> III. His desire and expectation of an answer of peace. He begs in faith (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hear my cry, O God! attend unto my prayer;</hi> that is, let me have the present comfort of knowing that I am heard (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Ps. xx. 6</reference>), and in due time let me have that which I pray for." <div eID="gen11508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11509" type="x-p"/> IV. The ground of this expectation, and the plea he uses to enforce his petition (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast been a shelter for me;</hi> I have found in thee a rock higher than I: therefore I trust thou wilt still lead me to that rock." Note, Past experiences of the benefit of trusting in God, as they should engage us still to keep close to him, so they should encourage us to hope that it will not be in vain. "Thou hast been my <hi type="italic">strong tower from the enemy,</hi> and thou art as strong a ever, and thy name is as much a refuge to the righteous as ever it was." <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Prov. xviii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen11509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11510" type="x-p"/> V. His resolution to continue in the way of duty to God and dependence on him, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.4">v. 4</reference>. 1. The service of God shall be his constant work and business. All those must make it so who expect to find God their shelter and strong tower: none but his menial servants have the benefit of his protection. <hi type="italic">I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever.</hi> David was now banished from the tabernacle, which was his greatest grievance, but he is assured that God by his providence would bring him back to his tabernacle, because he had by his grace wrought in him such a kindness for the tabernacle as that he was resolved to make it his perpetual residence, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>. He speaks of abiding in it <hi type="italic">for ever</hi> because that tabernacle was a type and figure of heaven, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.8-Heb.9.9">Heb. ix. 8, 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">24</reference>. Those that dwell in God's tabernacle, as it is a house of duty, during their short <hi type="italic">ever</hi> on earth, shall dwell in that tabernacle which is the house of glory during an endless <hi type="italic">ever.</hi> 2. The grace of God and the covenant of grace shall be his constant comfort: <hi type="italic">I will make my refuge in the covert of his wings,</hi> as the chickens seek both warmth and safety under the wings of the hen. Those that have found God a shelter to them ought still to have recourse to him in all their straits. This advantage those have that abide in God's tabernacle, that in the time of trouble he shall there hide them.
entries.8714b6eeeef05adb72b8dc41d77090139d66eb8f: <div eID="gen11510" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mercies Recollected.</title> <div sID="gen11511" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> For thou, O God, hast heard my vows: thou hast given <hi type="italic">me</hi> the heritage of those that fear thy name. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thou wilt prolong the king's life: <hi type="italic">and</hi> his years as many generations. <hi type="super">7</hi> He shall abide before God for ever: O prepare mercy and truth, <hi type="italic">which</hi> may preserve him. <hi type="super">8</hi> So will I sing praise unto thy name for ever, that I may daily perform my vows. <div eID="gen11511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11512" type="x-p"/> In these verses we may observe, <div eID="gen11512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11513" type="x-p"/> I. With what pleasure David looks back upon what God had done for him formerly (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou, O God! hast heard my vows,</hi> that is, 1. "The vows themselves which I made, and with which I bound my soul: thou hast taken notice of them; thou hast accepted them, because made in sincerity, and been well pleased with them; thou hast been mindful of them, and put me in mind of them." God put Jacob in mind of his vows, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.13">Gen. xxxi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">xxxv. 1</reference>. Note, God is a witness to all our vows, all our good purposes, and all our solemn promises of new obedience. He keeps an account of them, which should be a good reason with us, as it was with David here, why we should perform our vows, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">v. 8</reference>. For he that hears the vows we made will make us hear respecting them if they be not made good. 2. "The prayers that went along with those vows; those thou hast graciously heard and answered," which encouraged him now to pray, <hi type="italic">O God! hear my cry.</hi> He that never did say to the seed of Jacob, Seek you me in vain, will not now begin to say so. "Thou hast heard my vows, and given a real answer to them; for <hi type="italic">thou hast given me a heritage of those that fear thy name.</hi>" Note, (1.) There is a peculiar people in the world that fear God's name, that with a holy awe and reverence accept of and accommodate themselves to all the discoveries he is pleased to make of himself to the children of men. (2.) There is a heritage peculiar to that peculiar people, present comforts, earnests of their future bliss. God himself is their inheritance, their portion for ever. The Levites that had God for their inheritance must take up with him, and not expect a lot like their brethren; so those that fear God have enough in him, and therefore must not complain if they have but little of the world. (3.) We need desire no better heritage than that of those who fear God. If God deal with us as he uses to deal with those that love his name we need not desire to be any better dealt with. <div eID="gen11513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11514" type="x-p"/> II. With what assurance he looks forward to the continuance of his life (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt prolong the king's life.</hi> This may be understood either, 1. Of himself. If it was penned before he came to the crown, yet, being anointed by Samuel, and knowing what God had spoken in his holiness, he could in faith call himself <hi type="italic">the king,</hi> though now persecuted as an out-law; or perhaps it was penned when Absalom sought to dethrone him, and force him into exile. There were those that aimed to shorten his life, but he trusted to God to prolong his life, which he did to the age of man set by Moses (namely, seventy years), which, being spent in serving his generation according to the will of God (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.36">Acts xiii. 36</reference>), might be reckoned <hi type="italic">as many generations,</hi> because many generations would be the better for him. His resolution was to abide in God's tabernacle for ever (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.4">v. 4</reference>), in a way of duty; and now his hope is that he shall abide before God for ever, in a way of comfort. Those abide to good purpose in this world that abide before God, that serve him and walk in his fear; and those that do so shall abide before him for ever. He speaks of himself in the third person, because the psalm was delivered to the chief musician for the use of the church, and he would have the people, in singing it, to be encouraged with an assurance that, notwithstanding the malice of his enemies, their king, as they wished, should live for ever. Or, 2. Of the Messiah, the King of whom he was a type. It was a comfort to David to think, whatever became of him, that the years of the Lord's Anointed would be as many generations, and that <hi type="italic">of the increase of his government and peace there should be no end.</hi> The Mediator shall abide before God for ever, for he always appears in the presence of God for us, and ever lives, making intercession; and, because he lives, we shall live also. <div eID="gen11514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11515" type="x-p"/> III. With what importunity he begs of God to take him and keep him always under his protection: <hi type="italic">O prepare mercy and truth which may preserve him!</hi> God's promises and our faith in them are not to supersede, but to quicken and encourage prayer. David is sure that God will prolong his life, and therefore prays that he would preserve it, not that he would prepare him a strong lifeguard, or a well-fortified castle, but that he would prepare mercy and truth for his preservation; that is, that God's goodness would provide for his safety according to the promise. We need not desire to be better secured than under the protection of God's mercy and truth. This may be applied to the Messiah: "Let him be sent in the fulness of time, in <hi type="italic">performance of the truth to Jacob and the mercy to Abraham.</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mic.7.20">Micah vii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.72-Luke.1.73">Luke i. 72, 73</reference>. <div eID="gen11515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11516" type="x-p"/> IV. With what cheerfulness he vows the grateful returns of duty to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">So will I sing praise unto thy name for ever.</hi> Note, God's preservation of us calls upon us to praise him; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> we should desire to live, that we may praise him: <hi type="italic">Let my soul live, and it shall praise thee.</hi> We must make praising God the work of our time, even to the last (as long as our lives are prolonged we must continue praising God), and then it shall be made the work of our eternity, and we shall be praising him for ever. <hi type="italic">That I may daily perform my vows.</hi> His praising God was itself the performance of his vows, and it disposed his heart to the performance of his vows in other instances. Note, 1. The vows we have made we must conscientiously perform. 2. Praising God and paying our vows to him must be our constant daily work; every day we must be doing something towards it, because it is all but little in comparison with what is due, because we daily receive fresh mercies, and because, if we think much to do it daily, we cannot expect to be doing it eternally.  <chapter eID="Ps.61"/> <div eID="gen11516" type="x-p"/>

entries.af3081ef3830183da3bd967c0801f4bdb0ab053b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6159"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 61</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.61.1-Ps.61.8">Psa 61:1-8</reference>. Neginah--or, Neginoth (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>, title). Separated from his usual spiritual privileges, perhaps by Absalom's rebellion, the Psalmist prays for divine aid, and, in view of past mercies, with great confidence of being heard.</title> <div sID="gen9422" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6159"/><hi type="bold">1-3. From the end--</hi>that is, places remote from the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.64">De 28:64</reference>). <div eID="gen9422" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a2c133c31af4e9c230049c92425c9272fc96a3b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6162"/><div sID="gen9427" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6162"/><hi type="bold">4. I will abide--</hi>So I desire to do (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.23.6">Psa 23:6</reference>).<div eID="gen9427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trust in the covert, &c.--</hi>make my refuge, in the shadow (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.7">36:7</reference>). <div eID="gen9428" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a43a4c69fbe8beb2eff241666790687eb50d0d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6163"/><div sID="gen9429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6163"/><hi type="bold">5. the heritage--</hi>or, part in the spiritual blessings of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.2-Ps.21.4">Psa 21:2-4</reference>).<div eID="gen9429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vows--</hi>implies prayers. <div eID="gen9430" type="x-p"/>
entries.02fb7363ff3e9edd7f11e9c581544ab29ed0fa1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6164"/><div sID="gen9431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6164"/><hi type="bold">6-7. the king--</hi>himself and his royal line ending in Christ. Mercy and truth personified, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.11">Psa 40:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">57:3</reference>. <div eID="gen9431" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fab07535039ae7158fb93aac60237f291bee370: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6166"/><div sID="gen9433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6166"/>8. Thus for new blessings will new vows of praise ever be paid. <chapter eID="Ps.61"/>

entries.dec414297e1c6608738dd0bce9d50b6b78853ab9: <div eID="gen20580" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20581" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20582" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20582" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20581" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20583" type="x-p"/> The psalmist's prayer for those who mere banished from their own land, and from the ordinances of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.1">Psa 61:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.2">Psa 61:2</reference>. He praises God for his past mercies, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.3">Psa 61:3</reference>; purposes to devote himself entirely to his service, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.4">Psa 61:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.5">Psa 61:5</reference>. He prays for the king, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.6">Psa 61:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.7">Psa 61:7</reference>; and promises to perform his vow to the Lord daily, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference>. <div eID="gen20583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20584" type="x-p"/> The title, To the chief Musician upon Neginath, נגינת. The verb נגן nagan signifies to strike or play on a musical instrument, especially one of the stringed kind; but the נגינות neginoth, as it is written in about thirty MSS., may signify either the players on the instruments or the instruments themselves. The Psalm appears to have been written about the close of the captivity, and the most judicious interpreters refer it to that period. On this supposition the notes are formed. <div eID="gen20584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20585" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20586" type="x-p"/> Hear my cry, O God - In the midst of a long and painful captivity, oppressed with suffering, encompassed with cruel enemies and isolent masters, I address my humble prayer to Thee, O my God.
entries.e405fe1088a611fa5be863b96041988f05f89f7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20587" type="x-p"/> From the end of the earth - ארץ arets should be here translated land, not earth, and so it should be in numerous places besides. But here it seems to mean the country beyond the Euphrates; as it is thought to do, <reference osisRef="Psa.65.5">Psa 65:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.65.8">Psa 65:8</reference>, called there also the ends of the earth or land. It may be remarked that the Jews were always more pious and devoted to God in their afflictions and captivities, than when in their own land, in ease and affluence. But who can bear prosperity? How many hearts filled with heavenly ardor in affliction and persecution have grown cold under the beams of the sun of prosperity! <div eID="gen20587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20588" type="x-p"/> Lead me to the rock that is higher than I - Direct me to a place of refuge and safety. It is a metaphorical expression; and Calmet interprets it of the liberty granted to the Jews by Cyrus to return to their own land. This was a privilege far higher than any thing they could expect. The fathers think Jesus Christ is meant by this high rock.
entries.af1ad9a31134703992afe0a9a42b0dda7d96d056: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20589" type="x-p"/> Those hast been a shelter for me - During the whole duration of the captivity God marvellously dealt with the poor Jews; so that, although they were cast down, they were not utterly forsaken.
entries.786215081c30c93c5446ecea1abdb705ae3bc206: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20590" type="x-p"/> I will abide in thy tabernacle - The greater portion of those Psalms which were composed during and after the captivity, says Calmet, had Levites and priests for their authors. Hence we find the ardent desire so frequently expressed of seeing the temple; of praising God there; of spending their lives in that place, performing the functions of their sacred office. There I shall sojourn; - there I shall dwell, - be at rest, - be in safety, - be covered with thy wings, as a bird in its nest is covered with the wings of its mother. These simple comparisons, drawn from rural affairs and ordinary occurrences, are more pleasing and consolatory in the circumstances in question, than allegories derived from subjects the most noble and sublime.
entries.aeeae4efc0e320eb172ef0eceeefecef94659adc: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20591" type="x-p"/> Hast heard my vows - Often have I purposed to be wholly thine, - to serve thee alone, - to give up my whole life to thy service: and thou hast heard me, and taken me at my word; and given me that heritage, the privilege of enjoying thee in thy ordinances, which is the lot of them that fear thy name. The Psalm seems to have been composed either after the captivity, or at the time that Cyrus published his decree in their favor, as has been remarked before.
entries.dbc4fdb06dd83edef03951f0e49e9fbdb69d688a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20592" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt prolong the king's life - The words are very emphatic, and can refer to no ordinary person. Literally, "Days upon days thou wilt add to the king; and his years shall be like the generations of this world, and the generations of the world to come." This is precisely the paraphrase I had given to this text before I had looked into the Chaldee Version; and to which I need add nothing, as I am persuaded no earthly king is intended: and it is Christ, as Mediator, that "shall abide before God for ever," <reference osisRef="Psa.61.7">Psa 61:7</reference>. Neither to David, nor to any earthly sovereign, can these words be applied.
entries.973462ea36225ca46c5e2ee0a94e92fd0ef1f857: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20593" type="x-p"/> He shall abide before God for ever - Literally, "He shall sit for ever before the faces of God." He shall ever appear in the presence of God for us. And he ever sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high; for he undertook this office after having, by his sacrificial offering, made atonement for our sins. <div eID="gen20593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20594" type="x-p"/> Prepare mercy and truth, which may preserve him - As Mediator, his attendants will ever be mercy and truth. He will dispense the mercy of God, and thus fulfill the truth of the various promises and predictions which had preceded his incarnation. There is an obscurity in this clause, חסד ואמת מן ינצרהו chesed veemeth man yintseruhu, owing to the particle מן man, which some translate who or what; and others, number thou, from מנה manah, to count. Houbigant, and he is followed by Bishop Lowth, would read מיהוה miyehovah, Mercy and truth from Jehovah shall preserve him. The AngloSaxon has, Mildheartedness, and soothfastness his, who seeketh? which is nearly the rendering of the old Psalter: Mercy and sothfastnes of him, wha sall seke? Dr. Kennicott says, מן man is a Syriasm; and should be translated quaesoutinam, I beseech thee, - I wish, - O that! On this very ground Coverdale appears to have translated, O let thy lovynge mercy and faithfulnes preserve him! The sense I have given above I conceive to be the true one.
entries.2b34b6e146c2b8b0dab0f58ad144a8a2615bf193: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20595" type="x-p"/> So will I sing praise unto thy name for evher - For the benefits which I have received, and hope to receive endlessly from thee, I will to all perpetuity praise thee. <div eID="gen20595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20596" type="x-p"/> That I may daily perform my vows - While I live, I shall יום יום yom, yom, "day by day," each day as it succeeds, render to thee my vows - act according to what I have often purposed, and as often promised. The Chaldee ends remarkably: "Thus I will praise thy name for ever, when I shall perform my vows in the day of the rederaption of Israel; and in the day in which the King Messiah shall be anointed, that he may reign." <div eID="gen20596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20597" type="x-p"/> The ancient Jews were full of the expectation of the Messiah; the Jews of the present day have given up their hope.  <chapter eID="Ps.61"/> <div eID="gen20597" type="x-p"/>

entries.70a81593432510454a90443ce5a22d9200f1a6bb: <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1-Ps.61.4">Psa 61:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9610" type="x-p"/> Hurled out of the land of the Lord in the more limited sense<note placement="foot">Just as in Num 32:29. the country east of Jordan is excluded from the name “the land of Canaan” in the stricter sense, so by the Jewish mind it was regarded from the earliest time to a certain extent as a foreign country (חוצה לארץ), although inhabited by the two tribes and a half; so that not only is it said of Moses that he died in a foreign land, but even of Saul that he is buried in a foreign land (<hi type="italic">Numeri Rabba</hi>, ch. viii. and elsewhere).</note> into the country on the other side of the Jordan, David felt only as though he were banished to the extreme corner of the earth (not: of the land, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.46.10">Psa 46:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">Deu 28:49</reference>, and frequently), far from the presence of God (Hengstenberg). It is the feeling of homelessness and of separation from the abode of God by reason of which the distance, in itself so insignificant (just as was the case with the exiles later on), became to him immeasurably great. For he still continually needed God’s helpful intervention; the enveloping, the veiling, the faintness of his heart still continues (עטף, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛tf</hi>, according to its radical signification: to bend and lay anything round so that it lies or draws over something else and covers it, here of a self-enveloping); a rock of difficulties still ever lies before him which is too high for his natural strength, for his human ability, therefore insurmountable. But he is of good courage: God will lead him up with a sure step, so that, removed from all danger, he will have rocky ground under his feet. He is of good courage, for God has already proved Himself to be a place of refuge to him, to be a strong tower, defying all attack, which enclosed him, the persecuted one, so that the enemy can gain no advantage over him (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Pro 18:10</reference>). He is already on the way towards his own country, and in fact his most dearly loved and proper home: he will or he has to (in accordance with the will of God) dwell (cf. the cohortative in <reference osisRef="Isa.38.10">Isa 38:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.21">Jer 4:21</reference>) in God’s tabernacle (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1">Psa 15:1</reference>) throughout aeons (an utterance which reminds one of the synchronous <reference osisRef="Ps.23.6">Psa 23:6</reference>). With גּוּר is combined the idea of the divine protection (cf. Arabic <hi type="italic">ǵâr ollah ,</hi> the charge or protegé of God, and Beduinic <hi type="italic">ǵaur</hi>, the protecting hearth; <hi type="italic">ǵawir</hi>, according to its form = גּר, one who flees for refuge to the hearth). A bold figure of this protection follows: he has to, or will trust, i.e., find refuge, beneath the protection of God’s wings. During the time the tabernacle was still being moved from place to place we hear no such mention of dwelling in God’s tabernacle or house. It was David who coined this expression for loving fellowship with the God of revelation, simultaneously with his preparation of a settled dwelling-place for the sacred Ark. In the Psalms that belong to the time of his persecution by Saul such an expression is not yet to be found; for in <reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">Psa 52:7</reference>, when it is desired that Doeg may have the opposite of an eternal dwelling-place, it is not the sacred tent that is meant. We see also from its second part that this <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1-Ps.61.8">Psa 61:1-8</reference> does not belong to the time of Saul; for David does not speak here as one who has drawn very near to his kingly office (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.40.8">Psa 40:8</reference>), but as one who is entering upon a new stage in it.
entries.0a63fbe2900fe2df8bcbbaf9a114d0535865dbf5: <reference osisRef="Ps.61.5-Ps.61.8">Psa 61:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen9610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9611" type="x-p"/> The second part begins with a confirmation of the gracious purpose of God expressed in Psa 61:5. David believes that he shall experience what he gives expression to in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.5">Psa 61:5</reference>; for God has already practically shown him that neither his life nor his kingship shall come to an end yet; He has answered the prayers of His chosen one, that, blended with vows, resulted from the lowly, God-resigned spirit which finds expression in 2Sa 15:25., and He has given or delivered up to him the land which is his by inheritance, when threatened by the rebels as robbers, - the land to which those who fear the covenant God have a just claim. It is clear enough that the receivers are “those who fear the name of Jahve;” the genitive relation describes the ירשּׁה as belonging to them in opposition to those who had usurped it. Or does ירשּׁה here perhaps mean the same as ארשׁת in <reference osisRef="Ps.21.3">Psa 21:3</reference>? Certainly not. נתן ירשּׁה ל is a customary phrase, the meaning of which, “to give anything to any one as his inheritance or as his own property,” is to be retained (e.g., <reference osisRef="Deut.2.19">Deu 2:19</reference>). God has acknowledged David’s cause; the land of Israel is again wrested from those to whom it does not belong; and now begins a new era in the reign of its rightful king. In view of this the king prays, in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.7">Psa 61:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference>, that God would add another goodly portion to the duration of his life. The words sound like intercession, but the praying one is the same person as in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.2">Psa 61:2</reference>-5. The expression מלכּא משׁיחא (the King Messiah) of the Targum shows to whom the church referred the word “king” after the extinction of the Davidic dynasty. The exalted tone of the wish expressed in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.61.7">Psa 61:7</reference></hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>) favours this without absolutely requiring it (cf. עולמים, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.5">Psa 61:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.5">Psa 21:5</reference>, and the royal salutation, 1Ki 1:31; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.4">Dan 2:4</reference>, and frequently). There ought (as also e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.8">Psa 9:8</reference>) not to be any question whether ישׁב in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference> signifies “to sit enthroned,” or “to sit” = “to abide;” when the person spoken of is a king it means “to remain enthroned,” for with him a being settled down and continuous enthronement are coincident. מן in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference></hi> is <hi type="italic">imperat. apoc.</hi> for מגּה (after the form הס, נס, צו). The poet prays God to appoint mercy and truth as guardian angels to the king (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">Psa 40:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.28">Pro 20:28</reference>, where out of pause it is צּרוּ; cf. on the other hand <reference osisRef="Ps.78.7">Psa 78:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Pro 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.2">Pro 5:2</reference>). Since the poet himself is the king for whom he prays, the transition to the first person in v. 9 is perfectly natural. כּן signifies, as it always does, so or thus = in accordance therewith, corresponding to the fulfilment of these my petitions, thankfully responding to it. לשׁלּמי is the infinitive of the aim or purpose. Singing praise and accompanying it with music, he will make his whole life one continuous paying of vows.  <chapter eID="Ps.61"/> <div eID="gen9611" type="x-p"/>

entries.ca3366233678ef4e0953ba658dd5db3371477173:
PSALM 61
This psalm begins with prayer, or, at any rate, with the brief record of a prayer, which David had preferred to God in a season of deep distress. It is chiefly occupied, however, with the praises of God, expressing his thankfulness for a miraculous deliverance which he had experienced from some imminent danger, and for his establishment upon the throne.
To the chief musician upon Neginoth, A Psalm of David.
Psalm 61:1-4
1. Hear my cry, O God! attend unto my prayer. 2. Prom the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is vexed: thou shalt lead me to the rock which is too high for me.
He represents himself as like a man climbing to get up into a place of safety, but who wants strength to get to it.
3. For thou hast been my hope, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy. 4. I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever; I will be safe under the covert of thy wings. Selah.
 
1. Hear my cry, O God! It is not exactly ascertained at what time this psalm was composed; but there seems to be some probability in the conjecture, that David had been for a considerable period in possession of the throne before he fell into the circumstances of distress which are here mentioned. I agree with those who refer it to the time of the conspiracy of Absalom;
It is generally agreed that this psalm refers to the history recorded in 2 Samuel 17:22, 24.
for, had he not been an exile, he could not speak, as in the second verse, of crying from the ends of the earth. By using the term cry, he would intimate the vehemency of his desire; and it is a word which expresses inward fervency of spirit, without reference to the fact whether he may have prayed aloud, or in a low and subdued tone. The repetition which is employed denotes his diligence and perseverance in prayer, and teaches us that we should not faint and become discouraged in this exercise, because God may not have immediately and openly testified his acceptance of our petitions. There can be no question that, by the ends of the earth, he refers to the place of his banishment, as being cut off from access to the temple and the royal city. By some, indeed, the words have been understood figuratively, as meaning, that he prayed from the lowest deeps of distress; but I can see no foundation for this. In a subsequent part of the psalm, he calls himself King, a title never assumed by him before the death of Saul, and from this circumstance we may at once infer, that the time referred to was that when he fled in trepidation from the fury of his son Absalom, and hid himself in the wilderness of Mahanaim, and places of a similarly solitary description. Mount Zion was the place where the ark of the covenant had been deposited, and it was the seat of royalty; and David, when banished from this, which was the principal and most eligible locality, speaks as if he had been driven to the uttermost parts of the earth. Living, though he did, under the shadows of a legal dispensation, he did not cease to pray, because removed to a distance from the temple; and how inexcusable must our conduct be, privileged as we are of God, and called to draw near by the way which has been opened through the blood of Christ, if we break not through every hinderance which Satan presents to our communications with heaven? Let those who may have been deprived of the hearing of the word, and the dispensation of the sacraments, so as, in a manner, to be banished out of the Church, learn from the example of David to persevere in crying to God, even under these solitary circumstances. He adverts, in what follows, to his grief and anguish. He adds the fact of his being shut up from every method of escape, that the grace of God might be made more apparent in his deliverance. The Hebrew word עטף, ataph, which I have translated vexed, means occasionally to cover, or involve, which has led some to render the clause, while my heart is turned about; that is, tossed hither and thither, or agitated. This is a harsh translation. Others read with more propriety, while my heart is involved in cares and troubles, or overwhelmed.
This last translation is omitted in the French version, perhaps through inadvertency.
I have adopted a simpler rendering, although I would not be understood as denying the metaphor, to which they suppose that there is an allusion. The clause, there can be no question, is inserted to intimate that he was not prevented by trouble from having recourse to God. Notice was taken already of the outward trial to which he was subjected, in distance from the sanctuary, and of his rising above this, so as to direct his cry to God; and in the words before us, we have his confession that he was far from being stoically insensible, being conscious of a severe inward struggle with grief and perplexity of mind. It is the duty, then, of believers, when oppressed with heaviness and spiritual distress, to make only the more strenuous efforts for breaking through these obstacles in their approaches to God. His prayer is, that God would bring him to that safety from which he seems to be excluded. By a rock or citadel, he means, in general, secure protection, from which he complains of being shut out, as it was impossible to reach it unless he were raised by the hand of God. In looking round him, it seemed as if every place of shelter and safety were lifted up above his head and rendered inaccessible. He was cut off from all help, and yet, hopeless as deliverance appeared, he had no doubt of his safety, should God only extend his hand for interposition. This is the plain meaning of the passage, when divested of figure, that God was able to rescue him from danger, though all other help should be withdrawn, and the whole world should stand between him and deliverance; a truth which we would do well to consider seriously. In looking for deliverance from God, we must beware of yielding to the suggestions of sense; we should remember that he does not always work by apparent means, but delivers us when he chooses by methods inscrutable to reason. If we attempt to prescribe any one particular line of procedure, we do no less than wilfully limit his almighty power.

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. LXI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>To the chief musician upon Neginah, <ns0:hi>a Psalm</ns0:hi> of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The occasion of this <ns0:hi>Psalm,</ns0:hi> was some great Distress of <ns0:hi>David's;</ns0:hi> Either by <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> or by <ns0:hi>Absalom;</ns0:hi> though it might be Composed some time after it was past.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 HEar my cry, O God, attend unto my prayer.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 From the end of the earth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>of the Land:</ns0:hi> To which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was driven by the Tyranny of his Enemies.</ns0:note> will I cry un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> is higher than I <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Convey me into some high and secure Fortress, which I could not reach without thy Succour, and where mine Enemies cannot come at me. He alludes to their Custom of securing themselves in Rocks, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 13. 6. &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 For thou hast been a shelter for me, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> a strong tower from the enemy.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">I shall, I doubt not, be restored to the Tabernacle; from which I am now banished, and, according to the desire of my Heart, worship and enjoy thee there all my days.</ns0:note>: I will <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> make my Refuge.</ns0:note> trust in the covert of thy wings <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In the mean time, whilst I am in Danger and Trouble, I will cast my self upon thy Protection with full Confidence.</ns0:note>, Selah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 For thou, O God, hast heard my vows <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">My servent Prayers, attended with many Vows and Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mises, as was usual, especially in Cases of great Danger or Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fficulty. <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 28. 20. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 11. 30, 31.</ns0:note>: thou hast given <ns0:hi>me</ns0:hi> the heritage of those that fear thy name <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Thou hast allot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed me my Portion, with and amongst them that Fear and Worship thee, who are the <ns0:hi>Excellent</ns0:hi> ones, <ns0:hi>in whom is all my Delight:</ns0:hi> And upon that Account I must acknowledge it to thy Praise, that <ns0:hi>the Lines are fallen to me in Pleasant places; Yea, I have a goodly Heritage, Psal.</ns0:hi> 16. 3. 6. Thou hast granted me this singular Mercy, to live in God's Land, and to enjoy his Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sence and Favour, and to Worship in his Tabernacle; which is the Heritage that I and all that Fear thee, prize and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sire above all things in the World.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> thou shalt add days to the days of the King.</ns0:note> Thou wilt prolong the kings life <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) My Life. He calls himself <ns0:hi>King;</ns0:hi> Either, 1. Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he was actually <ns0:hi>King,</ns0:hi> though <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> Usurped the Throne: Or, 2. Because he was designed and anointed to be King; and by calling himself <ns0:hi>King,</ns0:hi> he supports himself un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der his present straits, and declares his Confidence in God's promise of the Kingdom to him. Yet we must not think that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> did commonly and publickly Call, or own himself to be <ns0:hi>King,</ns0:hi> which had neither been True, nor Covenient for his Affairs: But this Psalm, either was not Composed whilst <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> lived, or, at least, was Penned onely for his private use and Comfort, and not <ns0:hi>Committed to the chief Musician;</ns0:hi> which in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed it could not be till <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had the Kingdom, and the In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spection of the sacred Musick and service of the Tabernacle.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> his years <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The years of my Life and Reign.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> as Gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration and Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neration.</ns0:note> as many generations <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As long as if I had a Lease of it for many Ages. Thus he speaks; Partly, because his Kingdom was not like <ns0:hi>Saul's,</ns0:hi> a matter of one Age, expiring with his Life, but Established to him, and his Heirs for ever: and Partly, because Christ, his Son and Heir, should actually, and in his own Person possess the Kingdom for ever.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 He shall abide <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>sit,</ns0:hi> to wit, in the Throne, <ns0:hi>Ier:</ns0:hi> 13. 13. Living and Ruling as in God's Presence, and serving God with his Royal Power, and Worshiping him in his Tabernacle.</ns0:note> before God <ns0:hi>l</ns0:hi> for ever: O prepare <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Order</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>appoint,</ns0:hi> as this Word signifies, <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> 1. 17. and 4. 6.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Pro. 20. 28.</ns0:note> mercy and truth <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 1. The graces of <ns0:hi>Mercy</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Compassion,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Truth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness;</ns0:hi> which are the great supporters of Thrones, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 20. 28. and 29. 14. Or rather, 2. Thy Mercy and Truth, (<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The Effects of them. Thy <ns0:hi>Truth</ns0:hi> in giving me those Mercies, which thou hast promised to me: and thy <ns0:hi>Mercy</ns0:hi> in giving me such further Blessings, as I need, and thou <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eest fit to give me.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> may pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 So will I sing <ns0:hi>praise</ns0:hi> unto thy name for e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver, that I may daily perform my vows <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That so I may pay unto thee those Services and Sacrifices, which I vowed to thee when I was in Trouble.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
